sectionTitle: Carbon compounds as fuels and feedstock

specStatements.text: Crude oil is a finite resource found in rocks. Crude oil is the remains of an ancient biomass consisting mainly of plankton that was buried in mud.
Crude oil is a mixture of a very large number of compounds. Most of the compounds in crude oil are hydrocarbons, which are molecules made up of hydrogen and carbon atoms only.
Most of the hydrocarbons in crude oil are hydrocarbons called alkanes. The general formula for the homologous series of alkanes is Cₙ H₂ₙ₊₂
The first four members of the alkanes are methane, ethane, propane and butane.
Alkane molecules can be represented in the following forms:
C₂ H₆ or
Students should be able to recognise substances as alkanes given their formulae in these forms.
Students do not need to know the names of specific alkanes other than methane, ethane, propane and butane.
The many hydrocarbons in crude oil may be separated into fractions, each of which contains molecules with a similar number of carbon atoms, by fractional distillation.
The fractions can be processed to produce fuels and feedstock for the petrochemical industry.
Many of the fuels on which we depend for our modern lifestyle, such as petrol, diesel oil, kerosene, heavy fuel oil and liquefied petroleum gases, are produced from crude oil.
Many useful materials on which modern life depends are produced by the petrochemical industry, such as solvents, lubricants, polymers, detergents.
The vast array of natural and synthetic carbon compounds occur due to the ability of carbon atoms to form families of similar compounds.
Students should be able to explain how fractional distillation works in terms of evaporation and condensation.
Knowledge of the names of other specific fractions or fuels is not required.
Some properties of hydrocarbons depend on the size of their molecules, including boiling point, viscosity and flammability. These properties influence how hydrocarbons are used as fuels.
Students should be able to recall how boiling point, viscosity and flammability change with increasing molecular size.
The combustion of hydrocarbon fuels releases energy. During combustion, the carbon and hydrogen in the fuels are oxidised. The complete combustion of a hydrocarbon produces carbon dioxide and water.
Students should be able to write balanced equations for the complete combustion of hydrocarbons with a given formula.
Knowledge of trends in properties of hydrocarbons is limited to:
boiling points
viscosity
flammability.
Hydrocarbons can be broken down (cracked) to produce smaller, more useful molecules.
Cracking can be done by various methods including catalytic cracking and steam cracking.
Students should be able to describe in general terms the conditions used for catalytic cracking and steam cracking.
The products of cracking include alkanes and another type of hydrocarbon called alkenes.
Alkenes are more reactive than alkanes and react with bromine water, which is used as a test for alkenes.
Students should be able to recall the colour change when bromine water reacts with an alkene.
There is a high demand for fuels with small molecules and so some of the products of cracking are useful as fuels.
Alkenes are used to produce polymers and as starting materials for the production of many other chemicals.
Students should be able to balance chemical equations as examples of cracking given the formulae of the reactants and products.
Students should be able to give examples to illustrate the usefulness of cracking. They should also be able to explain how modern life depends on the uses of hydrocarbons.
(For Combined Science: Trilogy and Synergy students do not need to know the formulae or names of individual alkenes.)

scopeNotes.statement: Students do not need to know the names of specific alkanes other than methane, ethane, propane and butane.
scopeNotes.howHonoured: Only methane, ethane, propane and butane are named as alkanes anywhere in this content. Larger alkanes appear only as formulae that are supplied in the question itself (for example C₅H₁₂, C₈H₁₈, C₁₀H₂₂), so a student never has to know or produce a name such as pentane or octane. No item asks students to name an alkane from a formula beyond the first four, and no distractor rewards or punishes knowing such a name.

scopeNotes.statement: Knowledge of the names of other specific fractions or fuels is not required.
scopeNotes.howHonoured: The only fuels named are the five the specification itself lists: petrol, diesel oil, kerosene, heavy fuel oil and liquefied petroleum gases. No item requires students to name bitumen, naphtha, paraffin wax or any other fraction, and where a fraction has to be referred to it is described by the size of its molecules or by where it leaves the column, not by a name students would have to learn.

scopeNotes.statement: Knowledge of trends in properties of hydrocarbons is limited to:
scopeNotes.howHonoured: Exactly three trends are taught and tested: how boiling point, viscosity and flammability change as the molecules get larger. No other property is trended – there is no work on density, colour, energy released per gram, ignition temperature values or intermolecular forces – and no numerical boiling point or viscosity data has to be recalled.

Boiling point is taught only as a direction of change: the larger the hydrocarbon molecule, the higher its boiling point. Students are asked to use that trend to decide which fraction condenses where, and nothing more. No boiling point values have to be recalled and the trend is not explained in terms of intermolecular forces, which lies outside this section.

Viscosity is taught only as a direction of change: the larger the hydrocarbon molecule, the more viscous (the less easily it flows) the liquid is. Students meet viscosity as a qualitative description of how runny a fuel is; no viscosity units, measurements or calculations are used.

Flammability is taught only as a direction of change: the larger the hydrocarbon molecule, the less flammable it is – the harder it is to ignite. Students link this to why small-molecule fractions make good fuels for engines. No ignition temperatures are quoted and no mechanism for ignition is taught.

scopeNotes.statement: (For Combined Science: Trilogy and Synergy students do not need to know the formulae or names of individual alkenes.)
scopeNotes.howHonoured: No item in this section requires a student to recall the name or the formula of any individual alkene. Alkenes are treated here as a type of hydrocarbon produced by cracking, which is more reactive than an alkane and decolourises bromine water. Where an alkene formula such as C₂H₄ is needed – in balancing a cracking equation, which the specification requires to be done from given formulae – the formula is supplied in the stem or is recoverable by balancing alone, so Combined Science students are never disadvantaged.

concepts.definition: A finite resource found in rocks. It is the remains of an ancient biomass consisting mainly of plankton that was buried in mud millions of years ago.

A resource that is being used up much faster than it is being formed, so the supply available to us will run out. Crude oil is finite, which is why the compounds obtained from it have to be used carefully.
Crude oil is a mixture of a very large number of compounds. The compounds are not chemically joined to each other, so they can be separated by a physical process such as fractional distillation.

A molecule made up of hydrogen and carbon atoms only. If a molecule contains any other element, such as oxygen or nitrogen, it is not a hydrocarbon. Most of the compounds in crude oil are hydrocarbons.
The type of hydrocarbon that makes up most of crude oil. The general formula for the homologous series of alkanes is CₙH₂ₙ₊₂, so an alkane with n carbon atoms has (2n + 2) hydrogen atoms.
A family of compounds that can be described by the same general formula, so each member differs from the next by a fixed step. The alkanes are the homologous series with the general formula CₙH₂ₙ₊₂.
Methane CH₄, ethane C₂H₆, propane C₃H₈ and butane C₄H₁₀. Each fits CₙH₂ₙ₊₂: for propane, n = 3 and (2 × 3) + 2 = 8 hydrogen atoms.
A way of representing a molecule using symbols and numbers to show how many atoms of each element it contains, for example C₂H₆ for ethane. It shows the numbers of atoms but not how they are joined.

A way of representing a molecule by drawing every atom and showing every covalent bond as a line. The displayed formula of ethane shows two carbon atoms joined by a single bond, with three hydrogen atoms bonded to each carbon.

concepts.term: Recognising an alkane from its formula
concepts.definition: Count the carbon atoms, work out (2n + 2) and compare with the number of hydrogen atoms. C₅H₁₂ is an alkane because (2 × 5) + 2 = 12; C₅H₁₀ is not, because it has two hydrogen atoms too few.
The industrial process that separates the many hydrocarbons in crude oil into fractions. It works because the hydrocarbons have different boiling points, and no new substances are made.

A part of the crude oil separated out by fractional distillation. A fraction is still a mixture, but it contains molecules with a similar number of carbon atoms and therefore a similar range of boiling points.

The oil is heated so that it evaporates, and the vapours pass into a column that is hot at the bottom and cooler at the top. A vapour rises until it reaches a level where the temperature is below its boiling point, where it condenses and is collected.

A raw material supplied to an industrial process so that it can be made into other substances. Fractions from crude oil are processed to give feedstock for the petrochemical industry as well as fuels.
Many of the fuels we depend on for our modern lifestyle are produced from crude oil, including petrol, diesel oil, kerosene, heavy fuel oil and liquefied petroleum gases.
The industry that uses feedstock from crude oil to make useful materials on which modern life depends, such as solvents, lubricants, polymers and detergents.

concepts.term: Why there are so many carbon compounds
concepts.definition: The vast array of natural and synthetic carbon compounds occurs because carbon atoms can form families of similar compounds, each family sharing a general formula, as the alkanes do.

As hydrocarbon molecules get larger, their boiling point increases. Fractions with the largest molecules therefore condense near the bottom of the column and those with the smallest molecules leave the top as gases.
As hydrocarbon molecules get larger, viscosity increases: the liquid becomes thicker and flows less easily. Small-molecule fractions are runny; large-molecule fractions are thick and sticky.
As hydrocarbon molecules get larger, flammability decreases: the fuel becomes harder to ignite. Fractions with small molecules ignite easily, which is why they are useful as fuels for engines.
Burning a hydrocarbon fuel releases energy. During combustion the carbon and the hydrogen in the fuel are oxidised, and complete combustion produces carbon dioxide and water.

Balance carbon first using CO₂, then hydrogen using H₂O, then oxygen using O₂. For propane: C₃H₈ + 5O₂ → 3CO₂ + 4H₂O. Only the big numbers in front may be changed, never the small numbers inside a formula.

A process in which hydrocarbons are broken down into smaller, more useful molecules. One larger molecule breaks into smaller ones, so the atoms present before and after are the same and the equation balances.
A method of cracking in which the hydrocarbons are heated until they vaporise and the vapour is then passed over a hot catalyst, where the molecules break down.
A method of cracking in which the vaporised hydrocarbons are mixed with steam and heated to a very high temperature, breaking the molecules down without a catalyst.
A type of hydrocarbon produced along with alkanes when hydrocarbons are cracked. Alkenes are more reactive than alkanes, and they react with bromine water.
The test used for alkenes. Bromine water is orange; when it is shaken with an alkene it reacts and turns colourless, whereas with an alkane it stays orange.

There is a high demand for fuels with small molecules, and the fractions with larger molecules are produced in greater amounts than they are needed. Cracking turns those larger molecules into products that are useful as fuels.
Alkenes are used to produce polymers and as starting materials for the production of many other chemicals, which is the second reason the products of cracking are valuable.

misconceptions.question: Where did the crude oil in rocks come from?
misconceptions.correct: It is the remains of an ancient biomass consisting mainly of plankton that was buried in mud.
misconceptions.misconception: Crude oil is made from dinosaurs and other big animals that died and rotted underground.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Fossil fuels are linked with fossils, and dinosaurs are the fossils children meet first, so the words become attached to each other.
misconceptions.correction: The specification is precise: crude oil is the remains of an ancient biomass consisting mainly of plankton – tiny marine organisms – that was buried in mud. It is coal, not oil, that comes mainly from land plants; large animals contributed effectively nothing.

misconceptions.question: New crude oil is still forming today, so why is it called finite?
misconceptions.correct: It is being used up enormously faster than it forms, so the supply available to us will run out.
misconceptions.misconception: Crude oil cannot be finite, because it is still being made underground all the time.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Students hear that oil is 'still forming' and treat any ongoing formation as enough to make a resource renewable.
misconceptions.correction: A resource is finite when it is not being replaced at anything like the rate it is used. Crude oil took many millions of years to form and is being extracted in decades, so on any human timescale it is a finite resource.

misconceptions.question: Is crude oil a compound or a mixture?
misconceptions.correct: It is a mixture of a very large number of compounds, which is why it can be separated physically.
misconceptions.misconception: Crude oil is a single substance – that is why it all looks the same, thick and black.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Crude oil looks uniform, and students expect a named substance with one name to be one substance.
misconceptions.correction: Crude oil is a mixture of a very large number of compounds that are not chemically joined. That is exactly why fractional distillation, a physical process, can separate it.

misconceptions.question: Ethanol, C₂H₅OH, burns well as a fuel. Is it a hydrocarbon?
misconceptions.correct: No. A hydrocarbon contains hydrogen and carbon atoms only, and ethanol also contains oxygen.
misconceptions.misconception: Anything that burns as a fuel and contains carbon and hydrogen counts as a hydrocarbon.
misconceptions.whyItArises: The definition gets loosened to 'contains carbon and hydrogen' instead of 'contains carbon and hydrogen only', and fuel is treated as the deciding feature.
misconceptions.correction: The word 'only' is the whole definition. Hydrogen and carbon atoms only: one oxygen atom in the molecule is enough to make it something other than a hydrocarbon.

misconceptions.question: What is the general formula for the homologous series of alkanes?
misconceptions.correct: CₙH₂ₙ₊₂, so an alkane with n carbon atoms has (2n + 2) hydrogen atoms.
misconceptions.misconception: The alkane formula is CₙH₂ₙ – there are always twice as many hydrogens as carbons.
misconceptions.whyItArises: CₙH₂ₙ is easier to remember, and it is the formula of the other family students meet, so the two get swapped.
misconceptions.correction: CₙH₂ₙ is not the alkanes. For alkanes it is always CₙH₂ₙ₊₂: methane CH₄, ethane C₂H₆, propane C₃H₈, butane C₄H₁₀ – every one has two more hydrogen atoms than twice the carbons.

misconceptions.question: Methane, ethane, propane and butane – is that all the alkanes there are?
misconceptions.correct: No. There are many more alkanes; those four are simply the ones you are required to name.
misconceptions.misconception: There are only four alkanes, because those are the four in the specification.
misconceptions.whyItArises: A required list is read as a complete list, and no others are ever named in lessons.
misconceptions.correction: The alkanes are a homologous series that continues indefinitely, and crude oil contains alkanes with very many carbon atoms. You only need the names of the first four, but you must still recognise larger alkanes from their formulae.

misconceptions.question: Ethane can be written as C₂H₆ or drawn out with every atom and bond shown. Are these two substances?
misconceptions.correct: No. They are two ways of representing the same molecule; the drawn form also shows the bonding.
misconceptions.misconception: The drawn-out version must be a bigger molecule, because it has all those extra lines in it.
misconceptions.whyItArises: The lines are read as extra parts of the molecule rather than as the bonds between the atoms that are already counted in the formula.
misconceptions.correction: A displayed formula shows the same two carbon and six hydrogen atoms as C₂H₆. The lines are the covalent bonds holding those atoms together, not additional atoms.

misconceptions.question: Is the petrol fraction from a fractionating column a pure substance?
misconceptions.correct: No. A fraction is still a mixture, but of molecules with a similar number of carbon atoms.
misconceptions.misconception: Distillation gives you pure substances, so each fraction must be one single compound.
misconceptions.whyItArises: In the laboratory, distillation is used to purify a liquid, so the industrial process is assumed to do the same thing.
misconceptions.correction: Crude oil contains far too many compounds to separate one by one. Fractional distillation separates it into fractions, each containing molecules with a similar number of carbon atoms and so a similar range of boiling points.

misconceptions.question: Are new substances made during the fractional distillation of crude oil?
misconceptions.correct: No. The hydrocarbons are only separated; every molecule leaving the column was already there.
misconceptions.misconception: The column is hot and things change, so the hydrocarbons must react to form the fuels.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Heat is associated with chemical change, and the fractions come out looking very different from the crude oil that went in.
misconceptions.correction: Fractional distillation is a physical separation that depends on boiling points. It works by evaporation and condensation only; making new molecules from the fractions is a later step, such as cracking.

misconceptions.question: Where is a fractionating column hottest?
misconceptions.correct: At the bottom, where the hot crude oil vapour enters; it becomes cooler further up the column.
misconceptions.misconception: The top is hottest, because heat rises and the lightest gases come out of the top.
misconceptions.whyItArises: 'Heat rises' is remembered from everyday life and applied to the column without checking what it would mean for the separation.
misconceptions.correction: The column has a temperature gradient with the bottom hot and the top cool. Vapours rise, cool, and condense at the level where the temperature falls below their boiling point; if the top were hottest nothing would separate.

misconceptions.question: Is crude oil produced only for fuels?
misconceptions.correct: No. Fractions are also processed into feedstock for the petrochemical industry.
misconceptions.misconception: Crude oil is a fuel, so everything that comes out of the column is burned as a fuel.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Oil is met almost entirely as petrol and diesel, so its role as a chemical raw material is invisible.
misconceptions.correction: As well as fuels, the petrochemical industry uses feedstock from crude oil to make useful materials on which modern life depends, such as solvents, lubricants, polymers and detergents.

misconceptions.question: Which boils at the higher temperature, a small hydrocarbon or a large one?
misconceptions.correct: The large one. Boiling point increases as the hydrocarbon molecules get larger.
misconceptions.misconception: Petrol boils really easily, so petrol must be the one with the high boiling point.
misconceptions.whyItArises: 'High' gets attached to how readily a liquid boils rather than to the temperature needed to boil it.
misconceptions.correction: Boiling easily means a low boiling point: little heating is needed. Small molecules such as those in petrol have low boiling points; large molecules need much higher temperatures, which is why they condense low down the column.

misconceptions.question: Heavy fuel oil is described as more viscous than petrol. What does that mean?
misconceptions.correct: It is thicker and flows less easily than petrol; viscosity increases as molecules get larger.
misconceptions.misconception: More viscous means it flows more easily, so heavy fuel oil must be runnier than petrol.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Viscosity is a new word with no everyday anchor, so students guess the direction and often guess it the wrong way round.
misconceptions.correction: Viscosity is resistance to flow. High viscosity means thick and slow-flowing, like heavy fuel oil; low viscosity means runny, like petrol. The larger the molecules, the more viscous the liquid.

misconceptions.question: Which is easier to ignite, a fraction of small molecules or one of large molecules?
misconceptions.correct: The small molecules. Flammability decreases as the hydrocarbon molecules get larger.
misconceptions.misconception: Big molecules must be more flammable, because a bigger molecule holds more energy to release.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Energy released per molecule is confused with how easily the fuel catches fire, and 'more fuel' feels like 'burns better'.
misconceptions.correction: Flammability is about how readily a fuel ignites, not how much energy it stores. Large-molecule fractions are hard to light and are used where that matters; small-molecule fractions ignite easily and make good engine fuels.

misconceptions.question: What is produced by the complete combustion of a hydrocarbon?
misconceptions.correct: Carbon dioxide and water, because the carbon and the hydrogen are both oxidised.
misconceptions.misconception: Burning a fuel always gives carbon monoxide and soot as well – that is what smoke is.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Real fires are sooty and smoky, so the products of every combustion are assumed to include soot and carbon monoxide.
misconceptions.correction: Those are the products of incomplete combustion, when there is not enough oxygen. Complete combustion oxidises the carbon fully to carbon dioxide and the hydrogen to water, and produces nothing else.

misconceptions.question: Is water really a product when methane burns?
misconceptions.correct: Yes. The hydrogen in the fuel is oxidised to water, which leaves as an invisible vapour.
misconceptions.misconception: Only carbon dioxide comes out of a burning fuel; any water must have come from the air.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Water vapour is invisible as it leaves the flame, and carbon dioxide is the product students hear about constantly.
misconceptions.correction: The hydrogen atoms in the hydrocarbon have to go somewhere. During combustion both the carbon and the hydrogen in the fuel are oxidised, giving carbon dioxide and water: CH₄ + 2O₂ → CO₂ + 2H₂O.

misconceptions.question: How do you balance CH₄ + O₂ → CO₂ + H₂O?
misconceptions.correct: Put a 2 in front of O₂ and a 2 in front of H₂O: CH₄ + 2O₂ → CO₂ + 2H₂O.
misconceptions.misconception: Change the small numbers in the formulae until each side has the same atoms, giving H₄O₂.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Adjusting subscripts makes the atoms tally faster, and the equation then looks balanced.
misconceptions.correction: Changing a subscript changes the substance: H₄O₂ is not water and does not exist. Only the large numbers written in front of a formula may be changed when balancing.

misconceptions.question: How is cracking different from fractional distillation?
misconceptions.correct: Cracking breaks large molecules into smaller ones; distillation only separates the molecules.
misconceptions.misconception: Cracking is just the next stage of separating the crude oil into more fractions.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Both happen at an oil refinery and both involve heating, so the two processes merge into one idea.
misconceptions.correction: Fractional distillation is a physical separation and every molecule survives it unchanged. Cracking is a chemical change: a large hydrocarbon molecule is broken down into smaller, more useful molecules.

misconceptions.question: What conditions are used for catalytic cracking?
misconceptions.correct: The hydrocarbons are heated to vaporise them, then the vapour passes over a hot catalyst.
misconceptions.misconception: A catalyst is added to the oil and is used up as the molecules are broken apart.
misconceptions.whyItArises: The catalyst is treated as a reactant because it is essential to the process and is present throughout it.
misconceptions.correction: A catalyst speeds up a reaction without being used up. In catalytic cracking the vaporised hydrocarbon is passed over a hot catalyst, which is still there at the end and is not part of the equation.

misconceptions.question: What does the steam do in steam cracking?
misconceptions.correct: The vaporised hydrocarbons are mixed with steam and heated to a very high temperature.
misconceptions.misconception: The steam is the catalyst, and that is why no very high temperature is needed.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Any second substance in a process is assumed to be a catalyst, and cracking has just been met as something a catalyst does.
misconceptions.correction: Steam cracking uses no catalyst. The hydrocarbon vapour is mixed with steam and heated to a very high temperature, and it is that temperature that breaks the molecules apart.

misconceptions.question: What comes out of a cracker?
misconceptions.correct: Alkanes and another type of hydrocarbon called alkenes are both produced by cracking.
misconceptions.misconception: Cracking just chops the chain up, so all the products are smaller alkanes.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Cracking is pictured as cutting a chain into pieces, which would leave every piece the same kind of molecule.
misconceptions.correction: There are not enough hydrogen atoms in the original molecule for every product to be an alkane. The products of cracking include alkanes and alkenes, and it is the alkenes that make cracking so valuable.

misconceptions.question: Which is more reactive, an alkane or an alkene?
misconceptions.correct: The alkene. Alkenes are more reactive than alkanes and react with bromine water.
misconceptions.misconception: Alkanes must be more reactive, because they burn so well as fuels and are used everywhere.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Burning is the only alkane reaction students meet, and burning fiercely reads as being reactive.
misconceptions.correction: Reactivity here refers to how readily the molecules react with other substances such as bromine water. Alkenes are more reactive than alkanes, which is exactly why bromine water can be used to tell them apart.

misconceptions.question: What is the colour change when bromine water reacts with an alkene?
misconceptions.correct: Orange to colourless: the orange bromine water is decolourised by the alkene.
misconceptions.misconception: It goes from colourless to orange, because a positive test means a colour appears.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Most tests students meet produce a colour, so the direction of change is assumed rather than recalled.
misconceptions.correction: Bromine water is orange to start with. A positive result here is the loss of that colour: shaken with an alkene it turns colourless. With an alkane it stays orange.

misconceptions.question: A gas turns bromine water colourless. Could it be an alkane?
misconceptions.correct: No. Alkanes do not decolourise bromine water; it stays orange, so the gas is an alkene.
misconceptions.misconception: Every hydrocarbon decolourises bromine water, so the test cannot tell you which it is.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Alkanes and alkenes are both hydrocarbons made of the same two elements, so they are expected to behave alike.
misconceptions.correction: The test works precisely because they differ. Alkenes are more reactive than alkanes and react with bromine water, decolourising it; alkanes leave it orange.

misconceptions.question: Why are large hydrocarbon molecules cracked?
misconceptions.correct: There is a high demand for fuels with small molecules, so cracking makes more of them.
misconceptions.misconception: The big fractions are useless waste, so cracking is a way of getting rid of them.
misconceptions.whyItArises: The word 'useful' in 'smaller, more useful molecules' is read as meaning the starting material had no use at all.
misconceptions.correction: The larger fractions do have uses, but far more of them come out of the crude oil than are needed, while demand for small-molecule fuels is high. Cracking converts the surplus into products that are in demand.

misconceptions.question: What are alkenes used for?
misconceptions.correct: They are used to produce polymers and as starting materials for many other chemicals.
misconceptions.misconception: Alkenes are only useful as fuels, like everything else that comes out of crude oil.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Cracking is introduced as a way of making more fuel, so every product is assumed to be burned.
misconceptions.correction: Some cracking products are indeed used as fuels, but alkenes matter for a second reason: they are used to produce polymers and as starting materials for the production of many other chemicals.

misconceptions.question: Bromine water is decolourised. What does that look like?
misconceptions.correct: The orange colour disappears and the solution becomes colourless, like water.
misconceptions.misconception: The bromine water turns cloudy and milky white when the alkene reacts with it.
misconceptions.whyItArises: The limewater test for carbon dioxide gives a milky white result, and the two positive tests get confused.
misconceptions.correction: Milky white is limewater with carbon dioxide. Decolourised means the colour is lost: orange bromine water becomes colourless, and the solution stays clear throughout.

misconceptions.question: Coal formed from ancient forests. Did crude oil form the same way?
misconceptions.correct: No. Crude oil formed from an ancient biomass consisting mainly of plankton buried in mud.
misconceptions.misconception: All fossil fuels formed in the same way, from ancient forests of land plants.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Coal, oil and gas are taught together as fossil fuels, so one origin story is stretched to cover all three.
misconceptions.correction: They have different origins. Coal formed mainly from land plants; crude oil is the remains of an ancient biomass consisting mainly of plankton, which lived in the sea and was buried in mud.

misconceptions.question: What makes a resource finite?
misconceptions.correct: It is used up far faster than it is replaced, so the supply will eventually run out.
misconceptions.misconception: A resource is finite if you have to dig it out of the ground, like oil from rocks.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Finite resources are usually met as things mined from rock, so the location is mistaken for the reason.
misconceptions.correction: Being underground is not what makes a resource finite; the rate of replacement is. Crude oil took millions of years to form and is being used within a few generations, so it will run out.

misconceptions.question: Carbon dioxide contains carbon. Is it a hydrocarbon?
misconceptions.correct: No. A hydrocarbon contains hydrogen and carbon only, and carbon dioxide has no hydrogen in it.
misconceptions.misconception: Any compound with carbon in it counts as a hydrocarbon – the name is about the carbon.
misconceptions.whyItArises: The word hydrocarbon is heard as a word for carbon compounds in general, and the hydro- part is ignored.
misconceptions.correction: Both elements must be present and no others. Carbon dioxide contains carbon and oxygen, so it is not a hydrocarbon; C₄H₁₀ contains hydrogen and carbon only, so it is.

misconceptions.question: What does a general formula such as CₙH₂ₙ₊₂ tell you?
misconceptions.correct: It gives the pattern every member of the series follows, whatever the number of carbon atoms.
misconceptions.misconception: The general formula is just the formula of the first member of the family, CH₄.
misconceptions.whyItArises: General is read as meaning typical, so one familiar example is offered in place of a rule.
misconceptions.correction: A general formula is a rule with n in it, not the formula of one compound. Put n = 1 into CₙH₂ₙ₊₂ and you get CH₄; put n = 4 in and you get C₄H₁₀.

misconceptions.question: How can you tell from a formula whether a hydrocarbon is an alkane?
misconceptions.correct: Check it against CₙH₂ₙ₊₂: the hydrogen atoms must number exactly (2n + 2).
misconceptions.misconception: If there are more hydrogen atoms than carbon atoms in it, it must be an alkane.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Every alkane does have more hydrogens than carbons, so the easy check seems to work – until an alkene is tested.
misconceptions.correction: More hydrogens than carbons is true of alkanes but does not identify them: C₃H₆ and C₄H₈ pass that test and are not alkanes. Only (2n + 2) hydrogen atoms will do.

misconceptions.question: Are propane and butane the same thing?
misconceptions.correct: No. Propane is the third alkane, C₃H₈, and butane is the fourth, C₄H₁₀.
misconceptions.misconception: Propane and butane are two names for the same bottled camping gas.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Both are sold in gas bottles for the same purposes, so the names are treated as interchangeable.
misconceptions.correction: They are different alkanes with different formulae, and their place in the series follows the number of carbon atoms: propane has three, butane has four.

misconceptions.question: How many bonds are shown in the displayed formula of ethane?
misconceptions.correct: Seven: six carbon–hydrogen bonds and one carbon–carbon bond joining the two carbon atoms.
misconceptions.misconception: There must be eight bonds, because there are eight atoms drawn in the molecule.
misconceptions.whyItArises: The symbols are counted instead of the lines, and each atom is assumed to bring one bond with it.
misconceptions.correction: Bonds join atoms, so they are not counted one per atom. In ethane each carbon forms four bonds and each hydrogen one, which gives six C–H bonds and one C–C bond: seven in all.

misconceptions.question: Where do plastics, solvents and detergents come from?
misconceptions.correct: They are made by the petrochemical industry from feedstock obtained from crude oil.
misconceptions.misconception: Those are laboratory chemicals, made from something else entirely – oil is only for fuel.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Plastics and detergents look nothing like crude oil, so the connection between them is invisible.
misconceptions.correction: The fractions from crude oil are processed to produce feedstock as well as fuels, and that feedstock is what the petrochemical industry turns into solvents, lubricants, polymers and detergents.

mcqs.stem: Crude oil is found in rocks. What is it the remains of?

options.text: Dinosaurs and other large animals that were buried in mud
options.rationale: 'Fossil fuel' is linked with fossils, and dinosaurs are the fossils students know best.

options.text: An ancient biomass consisting mainly of plankton buried in mud
options.rationale: This is exactly what the specification states: crude oil formed from an ancient biomass, mainly plankton, buried in mud.

options.text: Ancient forests of land plants that were buried under mud
options.rationale: This describes how coal formed; one fossil fuel's origin is stretched to cover them all.

options.text: Minerals in the rock that were changed by heat and pressure
options.rationale: Heat and pressure are part of the story, but crude oil began as living organisms, not as minerals.

mcqs.stem: Why is crude oil described as a finite resource?

options.text: It is still forming underground today, so it can never actually run out
options.rationale: Students hear that oil is still forming and treat any formation at all as making it renewable.

options.text: It is found in rock layers, and all resources dug from rocks are finite
options.rationale: The place it comes from is mistaken for the reason it will run out.

options.text: It is being used far faster than natural processes can replace it
options.rationale: Finite means the supply available to us will run out: formation takes millions of years, extraction takes decades.

options.text: It is an oily mixture, so only part of what is extracted is ever useful
options.rationale: Crude oil is a mixture, but that is about composition, not about the supply running out.

mcqs.stem: Which statement about crude oil is correct?

options.text: It is a single compound that can be given one chemical formula
options.rationale: Crude oil looks uniform and has one name, so students expect it to be one substance.

options.text: It is a mixture of the elements carbon, hydrogen and oxygen
options.rationale: Confuses a mixture of compounds with a mixture of elements, and adds oxygen to the hydrocarbons.

options.text: It is a compound of hydrogen and carbon called a hydrocarbon
options.rationale: Hydrocarbons are what crude oil mostly contains, but crude oil itself is a mixture of many of them.

options.text: It is a mixture of a very large number of different compounds
options.rationale: The specification states that crude oil is a mixture of a very large number of compounds, most of them hydrocarbons.

mcqs.stem: Which molecule is a hydrocarbon?

options.text: C₂H₅OH
options.rationale: It burns as a fuel and contains carbon and hydrogen, but the oxygen atom rules it out.

options.text: C₄H₁₀
options.rationale: It contains hydrogen and carbon atoms only, which is the definition of a hydrocarbon.

options.text: CO₂
options.rationale: Contains carbon, and the hydro- part of the word hydrocarbon is ignored.

options.text: CH₃Cl
options.rationale: Carbon and hydrogen are present, but so is chlorine, so it is not a hydrocarbon.

mcqs.stem: What is the general formula for the homologous series of alkanes?

options.text: CₙH₂ₙ
options.rationale: Simpler to remember, and it belongs to the other family of hydrocarbons students meet.

options.text: CₙHₙ₊₂
options.rationale: The 2n is misremembered as n, keeping only the '+2' part of the formula.

options.text: CₙH₂ₙ₊₂
options.rationale: This is the general formula given in the specification; an alkane with n carbons has (2n + 2) hydrogens.

options.text: CH₄
options.rationale: Gives the formula of the first member instead of the rule for the whole series.

mcqs.stem: Which formula is an alkane?

options.text: C₅H₁₀
options.rationale: Twice the number of carbons, which is what a student using CₙH₂ₙ would pick.

options.text: C₅H₁₂
options.rationale: (2 × 5) + 2 = 12, so this fits CₙH₂ₙ₊₂.

options.text: C₄H₈
options.rationale: Again fits CₙH₂ₙ rather than CₙH₂ₙ₊₂.

options.text: C₃H₄
options.rationale: Has more hydrogen than carbon, which passes the wrong test for an alkane.

mcqs.stem: Which option correctly gives the name and the formula of the fourth member of the alkanes?

options.text: Butane, C₄H₈
options.rationale: The carbon count is right but the hydrogens follow CₙH₂ₙ instead.

options.text: Propane, C₃H₈
options.rationale: Propane and butane are met as the same bottled gas and are easily swapped.

options.text: Methane, CH₄
options.rationale: Falls back on the first member of the series instead of the fourth.

options.text: Butane, C₄H₁₀
options.rationale: Butane is the fourth alkane, so n = 4 and it has (2 × 4) + 2 = 10 hydrogen atoms.

mcqs.stem: How many carbon atoms and hydrogen atoms are there in one molecule of propane?

options.text: 3 carbon and 8 hydrogen
options.rationale: Propane is the third alkane, so n = 3 and (2 × 3) + 2 = 8 hydrogen atoms.

options.text: 3 carbon and 6 hydrogen
options.rationale: Uses CₙH₂ₙ instead of CₙH₂ₙ₊₂.

options.text: 2 carbon and 6 hydrogen
options.rationale: This is ethane; propane is placed second in the series by mistake.

options.text: 4 carbon and 10 hydrogen
options.rationale: This is butane, from counting propane as the fourth alkane.

mcqs.stem: Ethane can be written as C₂H₆ or drawn with every atom and every bond shown. Which statement is correct?

options.text: Both show the same atoms, but only the drawing shows the mixture
options.rationale: Confuses a representation of one molecule with the idea that oil is a mixture.

options.text: They show different molecules, since the drawing has extra bonds
options.rationale: The lines are read as extra parts of the molecule rather than as bonds.

options.text: They show different molecules, since only C₂H₆ is a real alkane
options.rationale: Treats the written formula as the substance and the drawing as something else.

options.text: Both show the same molecule, but only the drawing shows the bonding
options.rationale: A molecular formula counts the atoms; a displayed formula also shows how they are joined.

mcqs.stem: In the displayed formula of ethane, how many covalent bonds are shown?

options.rationale: Counts only the six bonds to hydrogen and forgets the bond joining the two carbons.
Six carbon–hydrogen bonds plus one carbon–carbon bond makes seven.
Counts the eight atoms in the molecule rather than the bonds between them.
Counts only the carbon atoms, not the bonds in the molecule.

mcqs.stem: What does fractional distillation do to crude oil?

options.text: Separates it into fractions of similar-sized molecules
options.rationale: Each fraction contains molecules with a similar number of carbon atoms.

options.text: Separates it into completely pure individual compounds
options.rationale: Laboratory distillation is used to purify, so the industrial process is assumed to do the same.

options.text: Reacts the hydrocarbons together to make useful fuels
options.rationale: Heat is associated with chemical change, and the products look very different.

options.text: Breaks the large molecules down into smaller molecules
options.rationale: Confuses distillation with cracking, which does break molecules down.

mcqs.stem: How does a fractionating column separate the hydrocarbons in crude oil?

options.text: Vapours rise and condense where it is hotter than their boiling point
options.rationale: The temperature gradient is reversed, so the condensation condition comes out backwards.

options.text: Heavier molecules sink through the column without ever evaporating
options.rationale: Pictures separation as settling by weight rather than by boiling point.

options.text: Vapours rise and condense where it is cooler than their boiling point
options.rationale: This is the explanation in terms of evaporation and condensation the specification requires.

options.text: Molecules react at each level to form the fraction collected there
options.rationale: Treats a physical separation as though new substances were being made.

mcqs.stem: Which fraction is collected near the bottom of a fractionating column?

options.text: One with small molecules and a very high boiling point
options.rationale: Keeps the idea of a high boiling point but attaches it to small molecules.

options.text: One with small molecules and a very low boiling point
options.rationale: These leave the top of the column as gases, not the bottom.

options.text: One with large molecules and a high boiling point
options.rationale: Large molecules have high boiling points, so they condense low down where it is hottest.

options.text: One with large molecules and a very low boiling point
options.rationale: Reverses the boiling point trend while keeping the molecule size right.

mcqs.stem: Fractions from crude oil are processed to give fuels and feedstock. What is feedstock?

options.text: A fuel that is burned to heat the fractionating column
options.rationale: Assumes everything from crude oil ends up being burned.

options.text: A waste fraction that is left over after the fuels are taken
options.rationale: Anything not sold as fuel is assumed to be waste.

options.text: A raw material used by industry to make other substances
options.rationale: Feedstock is the starting material supplied to the petrochemical industry.

options.text: A catalyst that speeds up reactions in the oil refinery
options.rationale: Any industrial term that is not a fuel is guessed to be a catalyst.

mcqs.stem: Kerosene and detergents are both obtained from crude oil. Which statement is correct?

options.text: Kerosene and detergents are both burned as fuels from crude oil
options.rationale: Crude oil is met almost entirely as fuel, so every product is assumed to be burned.

options.text: Kerosene comes from crude oil but detergents are made elsewhere
options.rationale: Detergents look nothing like oil, so the petrochemical link is invisible.

options.text: Kerosene is used as a fuel and detergents are petrochemicals
options.rationale: Kerosene is one of the fuels the specification names; detergents are made by the petrochemical industry.

options.text: Kerosene is a petrochemical product and detergents are the fuel
options.rationale: The two categories are known but attached to the wrong substances.

mcqs.stem: Which set of products is made by the petrochemical industry?

options.text: Solvents, lubricants, polymers and detergents
options.rationale: These are the examples the specification gives of useful materials modern life depends on.

options.text: Petrol, diesel oil, kerosene and heavy fuel oil
options.rationale: These are the fuels from crude oil, not the materials the petrochemical industry makes.

options.text: Plankton, sea mud, rocks and the crude oil itself
options.rationale: Confuses the raw origins of crude oil with the products made from it.

options.text: Bromine water, limewater and universal indicator
options.rationale: Treats these materials as laboratory chemicals unconnected with crude oil.

mcqs.stem: Why does such a vast array of natural and synthetic carbon compounds exist?

options.text: Carbon is the most abundant element found in the Earth
options.rationale: Abundance is not the reason, and the claim itself is not correct.

options.text: Carbon compounds are all made by the petrochemical industry
options.rationale: Confuses how compounds are manufactured with why so many can exist.

options.text: Carbon atoms can be separated by fractional distillation
options.rationale: Repeats a process from the topic instead of answering why the compounds exist.

options.text: Carbon atoms can form families of similar compounds
options.rationale: This is the reason the specification gives for the huge number of carbon compounds.

mcqs.stem: How do boiling point, viscosity and flammability change as hydrocarbon molecules get larger?

options.text: Boiling point falls, viscosity rises, flammability rises
options.rationale: Reverses the boiling point trend by confusing 'boils easily' with 'high boiling point'.

options.text: Boiling point rises, viscosity rises, flammability falls
options.rationale: This is the trend the specification requires students to recall.

options.text: Boiling point rises, viscosity falls, flammability rises
options.rationale: Takes more viscous to mean runnier, and links size with burning better.

options.text: Boiling point falls, viscosity falls, flammability falls
options.rationale: Assumes every property must change in the same direction together.

mcqs.stem: Heavy fuel oil has much larger molecules than petrol. Which statement is correct?

options.text: Heavy fuel oil is more viscous and harder to ignite
options.rationale: Larger molecules mean higher viscosity and lower flammability.

options.text: Heavy fuel oil is more viscous and easier to ignite
options.rationale: Gets viscosity right but assumes bigger molecules burn more readily.

options.text: Heavy fuel oil is more runny and harder to ignite
options.rationale: Takes 'more viscous' to mean flowing more easily.

options.text: Heavy fuel oil is more runny and easier to ignite
options.rationale: Both trends reversed, treating a big molecule as a better, thinner fuel.

mcqs.stem: Why are hydrocarbons with small molecules used as fuels in car engines?

options.text: They ignite easily and flow readily to where they are burned
options.rationale: Small molecules are the most flammable and the least viscous, which suits an engine.

options.text: They ignite easily and have very high boiling points
options.rationale: The flammability is right but the boiling point trend is reversed.

options.text: They are thick, which keeps the fuel in the engine longer
options.rationale: Confuses high viscosity with a useful property for a fuel.

options.text: They hold more energy because their molecules are smaller
options.rationale: Swaps flammability for a claim about energy content that is not correct.

mcqs.stem: What is produced by the complete combustion of a hydrocarbon?

options.text: Carbon dioxide and water
options.rationale: Complete combustion oxidises the carbon to carbon dioxide and the hydrogen to water.

options.text: Carbon monoxide and water
options.rationale: Assumes every fire produces the pollutants of incomplete combustion.

options.text: Carbon dioxide and hydrogen
options.rationale: The hydrogen is oxidised, so it leaves as water, not as hydrogen gas.

options.text: Carbon dioxide on its own
options.rationale: Water vapour is invisible, so it is easily left out of the products.

mcqs.stem: During the combustion of a hydrocarbon fuel, what happens to the carbon and the hydrogen?

options.text: Both are reduced, and the energy is taken in
options.rationale: Reverses oxidation and treats a fuel burning as an energy-absorbing change.

options.text: Only the carbon is oxidised; hydrogen escapes
options.rationale: Follows from thinking that carbon dioxide is the only product.

options.text: Both are oxidised, and energy is released
options.rationale: The specification states that the carbon and hydrogen in the fuel are oxidised and energy is released.

options.text: Only the hydrogen is oxidised; carbon is left
options.rationale: Comes from picturing the black soot of a smoky flame.

mcqs.stem: Which equation for the complete combustion of propane is correctly balanced?

options.text: C₃H₈ + 4O₂ → 3CO₂ + 4H₂O
options.rationale: The oxygen has not been balanced last: 8 O on the left, 10 O on the right.

options.text: C₃H₈ + 5O₂ → 3CO₂ + 4H₂
options.rationale: Leaves hydrogen as an element instead of oxidising it to water.

options.text: C₃H₈ + 5O₂ → 3CO₂ + 8H₂O
options.rationale: The 8 hydrogen atoms are copied straight across into 8 water molecules.

options.text: C₃H₈ + 5O₂ → 3CO₂ + 4H₂O
options.rationale: 3 C, 8 H and 10 O on each side, so the equation balances.

mcqs.stem: Balance the equation for the complete combustion of ethane: 2C₂H₆ + ?O₂ → 4CO₂ + 6H₂O. What replaces the ?

options.rationale: Counts the 14 oxygen atoms needed but forgets that each O₂ supplies two.
The right-hand side has 8 + 6 = 14 oxygen atoms, which is 7 O₂.
Supplies just enough oxygen for the 4CO₂, as though water were not a product.
Treats every product molecule as needing one O₂ molecule: 4 + 6 = 10.

mcqs.stem: What happens to hydrocarbon molecules during cracking?

options.text: Large molecules are broken down into smaller, more useful ones
options.rationale: This is what cracking is: breaking hydrocarbons down into smaller, more useful molecules.

options.text: Small molecules are joined together into larger useful ones
options.rationale: Reverses the process, confusing cracking with making a polymer.

options.text: Large molecules are separated out from the smaller ones
options.rationale: Confuses cracking with the physical separation done by distillation.

options.text: Large molecules are burned to release the energy in them
options.rationale: Assumes every process in a refinery exists to produce a fuel to burn.

mcqs.stem: Which conditions are used for catalytic cracking?

options.text: The hydrocarbons are vaporised and mixed with steam only
options.rationale: Describes steam cracking, which is the other named method.

options.text: The hydrocarbons are vaporised and passed over a hot catalyst
options.rationale: This is the general description of catalytic cracking required by the specification.

options.text: The hydrocarbons are cooled so the catalyst is not used up
options.rationale: Treats the catalyst as a reactant that must be protected.

options.text: The hydrocarbons are dissolved and a catalyst is added
options.rationale: Imports a laboratory picture of adding a catalyst to a solution.

mcqs.stem: Which conditions are used for steam cracking?

options.text: Mixing with steam and heating to a very high temperature
options.rationale: Steam cracking uses steam and a very high temperature, with no catalyst.

options.text: Mixing with steam, which acts as the catalyst for cracking
options.rationale: Assumes the steam must be a catalyst because it is the added substance.

options.text: Passing the vapour over a hot catalyst mixed with steam
options.rationale: Merges the two named methods into one process.

options.text: Bubbling steam through the cold liquid hydrocarbon
options.rationale: Leaves out the high temperature that actually breaks the molecules.

mcqs.stem: Which types of hydrocarbon are produced by cracking?

options.text: Smaller alkanes only
options.rationale: Cracking is pictured as chopping a chain into identical kinds of pieces.

options.text: Smaller alkenes only
options.rationale: Over-corrects, remembering only that cracking is how alkenes are made.

options.text: Alkanes and alcohols
options.rationale: Confuses alkenes with alcohols, which contain oxygen and are not hydrocarbons.

options.text: Alkanes and alkenes
options.rationale: The products of cracking include alkanes and another type of hydrocarbon called alkenes.

mcqs.stem: Bromine water is used to test for an alkene. What is the colour change?

options.text: Colourless to orange-red
options.rationale: Assumes a positive test must make a colour appear.

options.text: Orange to milky white
options.rationale: Confuses decolourising with the limewater test for carbon dioxide.

options.text: Orange to colourless
options.rationale: The alkene reacts with the bromine water, so the orange colour is lost.

options.text: Orange to a dark brown
options.rationale: A colour change is expected, but the reaction removes colour rather than deepening it.

mcqs.stem: Two gases are shaken with bromine water. Gas X leaves it orange; gas Y turns it colourless. What can be concluded?

options.text: X is the alkene, and it is the more reactive gas
options.rationale: Reads no colour change as the positive result for the test.

options.text: Y is an alkene and is more reactive than X
options.rationale: Alkenes react with bromine water and decolourise it; alkanes do not.

options.text: Both are alkenes, since both are hydrocarbons
options.rationale: Assumes all hydrocarbons behave identically with bromine water.

options.text: Y is an alkane, and alkanes are more reactive
options.rationale: Gets the reactive gas right but names the wrong family for it.

mcqs.stem: In the cracking reaction C₁₀H₂₂ → C₈H₁₈ + X, what is X?

options.text: C₂H₆
options.rationale: Assumes every product must be an alkane, which leaves the equation unbalanced.

options.text: C₂H₂
options.rationale: The hydrogen count is wrong; the atoms no longer balance.

options.text: C₂H₄
options.rationale: 10 − 8 = 2 carbon atoms and 22 − 18 = 4 hydrogen atoms, so X is C₂H₄.

options.text: CH₄
options.rationale: Picks a familiar small alkane instead of balancing the atoms.

mcqs.stem: In the cracking reaction C₁₂H₂₆ → 2C₂H₄ + Y, what is Y?

options.text: C₈H₁₆
options.rationale: Uses CₙH₂ₙ for the alkane, leaving two hydrogen atoms unaccounted for.

options.text: C₁₀H₂₂
options.rationale: Only one C₂H₄ has been subtracted, ignoring the 2 in front of it.

options.text: C₆H₁₄
options.rationale: Two carbon atoms too few, from subtracting the carbons incorrectly.

options.text: C₈H₁₈
options.rationale: 12 − 4 = 8 carbon atoms and 26 − 8 = 18 hydrogen atoms.

mcqs.stem: Why is cracking so useful to the petrochemical industry?

options.text: It gets rid of the large fractions, which have no uses at all
options.rationale: Reads 'more useful' as meaning the starting material was useless waste.

options.text: It turns every fraction of the crude oil into a burnable fuel
options.rationale: Assumes the only purpose of a refinery product is to be burned.

options.text: It separates the crude oil into more fractions than before
options.rationale: Confuses the chemical change of cracking with physical separation.

options.text: It meets the high demand for small-molecule fuels and makes alkenes
options.rationale: Cracking supplies fuels that are in demand and alkenes for polymers and other chemicals.

mcqs.stem: Alkenes from cracking are used to produce which of these?

options.text: Fuels only, since all cracking products are burned
options.rationale: Cracking is introduced as a way of making fuel, so every product is assumed to burn.

options.text: Polymers and starting materials for other chemicals
options.rationale: The specification states alkenes are used to produce polymers and as starting materials.

options.text: Plankton and the biomass that forms new crude oil
options.rationale: Confuses the origin of crude oil with what is made from it.

options.text: Pure fractions ready to be collected in the column
options.rationale: Muddles the products of cracking with the output of distillation.
